Ahab covets Naboth's vineyard (verses 1–4)

Naboth may once have been pleased to own a vineyard close to the royal palace.

But that location proved fatal to him.

Possessions often become traps, and living near powerful people can be dangerous.

Discontent is a sin that punishes itself, making people miserable through their own restless desires.

It also produces itself.

Discontent does not arise simply from outward circumstances, but from the mind.

Paul was content in prison; Ahab was discontent in a palace.

Ahab enjoyed every pleasure of Canaan, a beautiful and fruitful country.

He possessed the wealth of a kingdom, the luxuries of a royal court and the honor and authority of a throne.

Yet none of those things satisfied him without Naboth's vineyard.

Sinful desires continually expose us to distress.

People determined to complain can always find some cause for dissatisfaction, however comfortable their lives may be.

Jezebel has Naboth murdered (verses 5–16)

A wife ought to be a suitable helper to her husband.

But a cunning, unscrupulous and beloved spouse who acts as Satan's agent can bring terrible consequences.

Few rulers have ever given more wicked orders than those Jezebel sent to the leaders of Jezreel.

Naboth was to be murdered under the appearance of religion.

People have sometimes used religious language to cover even the most horrible wrongs.

The murder would also be made to appear lawful through the formal procedures of justice.

The episode reveals the cruelty of the wicked and Satan's influence among those who disobey God.

We should entrust our lives and earthly comforts to the Lord, because innocence does not always protect people from harm in this world.

Yet we may rejoice that all wrongs will finally be put right at the day of judgment.

Elijah announces judgment on Ahab (verses 17–29)

The apostle Paul lamented being sold under sin (Romans 7:14), like a helpless captive opposed to his own bondage.

Ahab was different.

He willingly sold himself to sin, choosing its dominion and loving it.

Jezebel encouraged him to continue in wrongdoing.

Elijah confronted Ahab and exposed his sin.

A person has reached a miserable condition when he regards God's word as his enemy.

It is even more desperate when he considers ministers his enemies simply because they tell him the truth.

Ahab adopted the outward clothing and behavior of a repentant person.

But his heart remained proud and unchanged.

He showed only what others could see.

His repentance was external, not genuine.

Nevertheless, his outward humiliation brought a delay in the announced judgment.

Let this encourage everyone who truly repents and sincerely believes the gospel.

If God granted a reprieve to a merely outward and partial penitent, surely a sincere believer may hope to go home justified, not merely reprieved.
classic_reading:
[1Kgs.21.1-1Kgs.21.4]
Chapter 21
Chapter Outline
Ahab covets Naboth's vineyard. | (1-4) |
Naboth murdered by Jezebel. | (5-16) |
Elijah denounces judgments against Ahab. | (17-29) |
Verses 1-4
Naboth, perhaps, had been pleased that he had a vineyard situated so near the palace, but the situation proved fatal to him; many a man's possessions have been his snare, and his neighbourhood to greatness, of bad consequence. Discontent is a sin that is its own punishment, and makes men torment themselves. It is a sin that is its own parent; it arises not from the condition, but from the mind: as we find Paul contented in a prison, so Ahab was discontented in a palace. He had all the delights of Canaan, that pleasant land, at command; the wealth of a kingdom, the pleasures of a court, and the honours and powers of a throne; yet all avails him nothing without Naboth's vineyard. Wrong desires expose men to continual vexations, and those that are disposed to fret, however well off, may always find something or other to fret at.
[1Kgs.21.5-1Kgs.21.16]
Verses 5-16
When, instead of a help meet, a man has an agent for Satan, in the form of an artful, unprincipled, yet beloved wife, fatal effects may be expected. Never were more wicked orders given by any prince, than those Jezebel sent to the rulers of Jezreel. Naboth must be murdered under colour of religion. There is no wickedness so vile, so horrid, but religion has sometimes been made a cover for it. Also, it must be done under colour of justice, and with the formalities of legal process. Let us, from this sad story, be amazed at the wickedness of the wicked, and the power of Satan in the children of disobedience. Let us commit the keeping of our lives and comforts to God, for innocence will not always be our security; and let us rejoice in the knowledge that all will be set to rights in the great day.
[1Kgs.21.17-1Kgs.21.29]
Verses 17-29
Blessed Paul complains that he was sold under sin, [Rom.7.14] Ro 7:14, as a poor captive against his will; but Ahab was willing, he sold himself to sin; of choice, and as his own act and deed, he loved the dominion of sin. Jezebel his wife stirred him up to do wickedly. Ahab is reproved, and his sin set before his eyes, by Elijah. That man's condition is very miserable, who has made the word of God his enemy; and very desperate, who reckons the ministers of that word his enemies, because they tell him the truth. Ahab put on the garb and guise of a penitent, yet his heart was unhumbled and unchanged. Ahab's repentance was only what might be seen of men; it was outward only. Let this encourage all that truly repent, and unfeignedly believe the holy gospel, that if a pretending partial penitent shall go to his house reprieved, doubtless, a sincere believing penitent shall go to his house justified.

Jehoshaphat makes an alliance with Ahab (verses 1–14)

Some genuinely godly people are naturally agreeable and accommodating.

That disposition can tempt them into friendship with open enemies of true religion.

It is especially dangerous because they may begin tolerating speech and behavior they ought to oppose.

A godly person should take faith along wherever he goes and should not be ashamed to acknowledge it among people who disregard it.

Jehoshaphat had not left his respect for God's word behind in Jerusalem.

He openly requested it even at Ahab's court.

Ahab's prophets used the name of Jehovah to please Jehoshaphat.

But their message of guaranteed success was designed to please Ahab.

False prophets may imitate true prophets' speech, but those with mature spiritual discernment can recognize the deception.

One faithful prophet of the Lord was worth all of them.

Worldly people have always been unreasonable about religion.

They expect preachers to adjust their doctrine to current fashions and the audience's taste, while still claiming divine authority for words people want to hear.

They treat someone who refuses such manipulation as foolish or uncivil, as though deceiving others were merely a sensible way of protecting one's interests.

Micaiah foretells Ahab's death (verses 15–28)

One of the greatest acts of kindness we can do for a person on a dangerous path is to warn that person clearly.

Micaiah described his vision to leave Ahab without excuse and teach everyone listening.

The scene is represented in language suited to human understanding.

We must not imagine that God needs to form new plans, consult angels or other creatures about what to do, or change his mind after receiving advice.

Nor should we imagine that God is the author of sin or the cause of a person telling or believing a lie.

Micaiah did not strike Zedekiah back when the false prophet struck him.

Zedekiah loudly claimed the Spirit's authority, as people ignorant of the Holy Spirit's true work often do.

Micaiah left him to discover his error when the prophecy was fulfilled.

People unwilling to let God's word correct their mistakes in time will eventually be undeceived by divine judgment, when it is too late.

We might be ashamed of calling our own difficulties severe if we considered what faithful servants of God have endured.

Yet a life without trouble may prove even more dangerous.

We can be drawn toward unfaithfulness and worldly conformity more easily through flattery and rewards than by threats.

Ahab dies in battle (verses 29–40)

Ahab intended to expose Jehoshaphat to danger while protecting himself.

See the reward of joining oneself to wicked people!

How could Ahab be trustworthy toward a friend when he had been unfaithful to God?

Jehoshaphat had told Ahab, “I am as you are.”

Now, because of the way they went into battle, he was mistaken for Ahab.

People who associate with evildoers risk sharing the harm that comes upon them.

God rescued Jehoshaphat, showing that though he was displeased with the alliance, he had not abandoned his servant.

The Lord is a friend who never fails when other friends do.

No one can hide from divine judgment.

God directed the arrow that struck Ahab.

Those whom God has appointed to die cannot escape that sentence by their own planning.

Ahab survived long enough to see part of Micaiah's prophecy come true.

He had time to feel himself dying and to remember the evil he had done.

What terror those memories must have brought!

Jehoshaphat's reign over Judah (verses 41–50)

Jehoshaphat's reign was among the best for both true devotion and prosperity.

He pleased God, and God blessed him.

Ahaziah's reign over Israel (verses 51–53)

Ahaziah's reign was very brief—less than two full years.

God brings some sinners to judgment quickly.

Scripture gives Ahaziah a terrible character.

He would not receive instruction or learn from the warnings he saw.

He imitated his wicked father and followed the counsel of his still-living mother, Jezebel, who was even more corrupt.

Children are deeply miserable when their parents not only pass on a sinful nature but actively teach them to increase their wickedness.

Parents who encourage their children toward destruction bring dreadful consequences upon their own households.

Hardened sinners can rush forward without fear along the same paths that have already brought others to eternal ruin.
classic_reading:
[1Kgs.22.1-1Kgs.22.14]
Chapter 22
Chapter Outline
Jehoshaphat makes a league with Ahab. | (1-14) |
Micaiah predicts the death of Ahab. | (15-28) |
Death of Ahab. | (29-40) |
Jehoshaphat's good reign over Judah. | (41-50) |
Ahaziah's evil reign over Israel. | (51-53) |
Verses 1-14
The same easiness of temper, which betrays some godly persons into friendship with the declared enemies of religion, renders it very dangerous to them. They will be drawn to wink at and countenance such conduct and conversation as they ought to protest against with abhorrence. Whithersoever a good man goes, he ought to take his religion with him, and not be ashamed to own it when he is with those who have no regard for it. Jehoshaphat had not left behind him, at Jerusalem, his affection and reverence for the word of the Lord, but avowed it, and endeavoured to bring it into Ahab's court. And Ahab's prophets, to please Jehoshaphat, made use of the name of Jehovah: to please Ahab, they said, Go up. But the false prophets cannot so mimic the true, but that he who has spiritual senses exercised, can discern the fallacy. One faithful prophet of the Lord was worth them all. Wordly men have in all ages been alike absurd in their views of religion. They would have the preacher fit his doctrine to the fashion of the times, and the taste of the hearers, and yet to add, Thus saith the Lord, to words that men would put into their mouths. They are ready to cry out against a man as rude and foolish, who scruples thus to try to secure his own interests, and to deceive others.
[1Kgs.22.15-1Kgs.22.28]
Verses 15-28
The greatest kindness we can do to one that is going in a dangerous way, is, to tell him of his danger. To leave the hardened criminal without excuse, and to give a useful lesson to others, Micaiah related his vision. This matter is represented after the manner of men: we are not to imagine that God is ever put upon new counsels; or that he needs to consult with angels, or any creature, about the methods he should take; or that he is the author of sin, or the cause of any man's telling or believing a lie. Micaiah returned not the blow of Zedekiah, yet, since he boasted of the Spirit, as those commonly do that know least of the Holy Spirit's operations, the true prophet left him to be convinced of his error by the event. Those that will not have their mistakes set right in time, by the word of God, will be undeceived, when it is too late, by the judgments of God. We should be ashamed of what we call trials, were we to consider what the servants of God have endured. Yet it will be well, if freedom from trouble prove not more hurtful to us; we are more easily allured and bribed into unfaithfulness and conformity to the world, than driven to them.
[1Kgs.22.29-1Kgs.22.40]
Verses 29-40
Ahab basely intended to betray Johoshaphat to danger, that he might secure himself. See what they get that join with wicked men. How can it be expected that he should be true to his friend, who has been false to his God! He had said in compliment to Ahab, I am as thou art, and now he was indeed taken for him. Those that associate with evil-doers, are in danger of sharing in their plagues. By Jehoshaphat's deliverance, God let him know, that though he was displeased with him, yet he had not deserted him. God is a friend that will not fail us when other friends do. Let no man think to hide himself from God's judgment. God directed the arrow to hit Ahab; those cannot escape with life, whom God has doomed to death. Ahab lived long enough to see part of Micaiah's prophecy accomplished. He had time to feel himself die; with what horror must he have thought upon the wickedness he had committed!
[1Kgs.22.41-1Kgs.22.50]
Verses 41-50
Jehoshaphat's reign appears to have been one of the best, both as to piety and prosperity. He pleased God, and God blessed him.
[1Kgs.22.51-1Kgs.22.53]
Verses 51-53
Ahaziah's reign was very short, not two years; some sinners God makes quick work with. A very bad character is given of him; he listened not to instruction, took no warning, but followed the example of his wicked father, and the counsel of his more wicked mother, Jezebel, who was still living. Miserable are the children who not only derive a sinful nature from their parents, but are taught by them to increase it; and most unhappy parents are they, that help to damn their children's souls. Hardened sinners rush forward, unawed and unmoved, in the ways from which others before them have been driven into everlasting misery.
